newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-THE SPORTING NEWS NOTICED JACKIE ROBINSON GRUDGINGLY.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-THE SPORTING NEWS NOTICED JACKIE ROBINSON GRUDGINGLY.

text.p: The Sporting News was the bible of baseball when Jackie Robinson broke the major-league colour line in 1947, an event momentous enough for the president of the United States to commemorate 50 years later.
But The Sporting News, which opposed Robinson's entry into the big leagues, was most remarkable in its annual "Baseball Guide and Record Book" for what it did not say about him.
In its summary of the 1947 season, Robinson is not mentioned until the 12th of 36 paragraphs, after a host of other issues little remembered today.
"Another significant event was the introduction of the Negro player for the first time in the modern history of the majors," it reads.

"Jackie Robinson, batting champion of the International League in 1946 as a second baseman for Montreal, earned the distinction of being the first Negro in the majors when Brooklyn brought him up a few days before the season opened and stationed him at first base.
"His sensational play earned him the award of Rookie of the Year."

Paragraph 13 notes the four other black players who were signed by major-league teams later in the year -- Larry Doby by Cleveland, infielder Henry Thompson and outfielder Willard Brown by the Browns, and pitcher Dan Bankhead by the Dodgers.

(Doby was the first black in the American League and played in 12 more seasons in the majors. Bankhead homered in his first at-bat, but pitched in just four games in 1947; he came back for two more seasons, 1950-51, totalling 52 game appearances in his career. Brown was released by St. Louis after a short trial, and Thompson went on to play eight seasons with the New York Giants.)

The first paragraph of the season summary crows over baseball's record attendance in 1947 -- but fails to speculate why. A major reason was Robinson, as fans turned out in throngs to see the exciting new player with the flashy, speedy new style.
Robinson's face is easily picked out in two pictures in the 618-page book -- in the Dodgers' team picture and in the World Series section, where he is shown caught in a rundown.

Robinson's regular-season and World Series statistics are of course included. (His totals in the seven-game World Series, won by the Yankees, were 7-for-27 for a .259 average, 3 runs scored, 2 doubles, 2 walks, 3 runs batted in and 2 stolen bases).
Even before compiling its 1947 record book, the St. Louis-based weekly had been forced to declare Robinson the Rookie of the Year.
"Robinson was rated and examined solely as a freshman player in the big leagues -- on the basis of his hitting, his running, his defensive play, his team value," The Sporting News said then.
"The sociological experiment that Robinson represented, the trail-blazing he did, the barriers he broke down did not enter into the decision."
